indicators.note: an unruly crowd is disordered, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A monarch ruling over a disorderly mob.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unruly' turns HORDE into a new order. HEROD was the king of Judea in the Gospel story.
explanation.definitionFit: Herod the Great was the Roman-appointed ruler of Judea, a biblical monarch.

clue.text: Having failed to win is punished

explanation.surface: A loser who also takes a thrashing afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A defeated side has been outplayed, and someone thrashed with a stick has been struck repeatedly as a penalty.

clue.text: Soccer player gets the bird for cheeky retorts

parts.note: a back is a defender in football
a chat is a small songbird such as the stonechat

explanation.surface: A footballer gets jeered for his insolent replies to the referee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets the bird' looks like being booed, but 'the bird' is a CHAT, a small songbird, and 'gets' joins it on.
explanation.definitionFit: Backchat is impudent answering back, the sort of cheeky replies a child gives to a parent.

indicators.note: involved suggests something tangled up, so these letters are twisted into another order

explanation.surface: A landlord's rent collector gets caught up in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges RENTMAN. 'scrap' looks like a fight, but here it is a leftover bit.
explanation.definitionFit: A remnant is a small leftover piece, such as an offcut of fabric.

indicators.note: something reformed has been made again in a new shape, so these letters are rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: A hefty man called Pat abruptly mended his ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reformed' rearranges BURLY and PAT together; 'got' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something happening without warning, at a sharp and unexpected moment.

clue.text: Guard what one says-it's a good maxim

parts.note: to watch is to keep guard over
a word is something spoken, as in giving one's word

explanation.surface: A sentry's password, one feels, is a sound principle to live by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A watchword is a slogan or guiding principle adopted as a rule of conduct.

clue.text: Thinks a great deal of events are badly organised

indicators.note: a badly organised set of things is in disarray, so these letters fall into another order

explanation.surface: Someone who admires events even when they are poorly run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly organised' rearranges EVENTS and ARE together.
explanation.definitionFit: To revere someone is to hold them in deep respect and high esteem.

indicators.note: breaking something up scatters its parts, so these letters are reassembled differently

explanation.surface: A ship on the point of falling apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to break up' looks like the vessel's fate, but it rearranges ABOUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A U-boat is a German submarine, a kind of seagoing craft.

clue.text: A slow mover may be fired

explanation.surface: Some sluggish creature that might get shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden slug is a famously sluggish mollusc, and a slug is also a bullet discharged from a gun.

parts.note: reads like concealing something from children, but kids are young goats and a hide is a pelt

explanation.definitionFit: This leather is made from the pelt of a goat, and young goats are called kids.

explanation.surface: A model boat-building plan.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorboat carried by a ship is one sense; the other is to set going or hurl forward, as with a rocket or new product.

clue.text: In certain charts it may indicate a mile

indicators.note: In tells the solver the letters sit inside the run of the words certain charts

explanation.surface: On some maps a small mark stands for a mile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like part of the surface's phrase but signals letters tucked within 'certain charts', across the word break. The surface is itself true: old maps used a scale of one to the mile.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordnance Survey maps were long drawn at a scale where this small unit of length on paper represented one mile.

clue.text: One who likes going out after dark needs own light to see

definitions.text: One who likes going out after dark

indicators.note: taken as what the letters require, a reworking, so these two words are reshuffled into another order

explanation.surface: A late-night reveller has to carry a torch to find the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needs' signals rearranging OWN and LIGHT; 'to see' rounds off the surface and joins nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who stays up and is lively late at night is named after the nocturnal bird.

clue.text: Procrastinate when it's time to get up

parts.note: tempo is musical time, the speed of a piece
to rise is to get up out of bed

explanation.surface: Someone dithering when the alarm says it is time to get out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when it's' links the definition to the wordplay; 'time' in music is TEMPO.
explanation.definitionFit: To temporise is to stall or delay a decision in order to gain time.

parts.note: Thomas Becket was Archbishop of Canterbury, murdered in 1170

indicators.note: first takes only the opening letter of thanked

explanation.surface: An archbishop gave thanks before a dramatist did.
explanation.walkthrough: BECKET is the medieval Archbishop of Canterbury; 'first' picks the T of 'thanked'.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Beckett was an Irish dramatist, author of Waiting for Godot.

indicators.note: ordered can mean arranged, so these letters are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: Important guests ordering pink gin at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' looks like asking for drinks, but it rearranges PINK and GINS.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingpins are the most important people in a group, the big shots.

parts.note: reads as a bare remark about tireless horses, with 'yet' hinting at still or remaining, the sense behind the name

explanation.definitionFit: Racehorses with great stamina, suited to long distances, are named for their ability to last the course.

clue.text: Varieties of meat for a fellow sportsman

indicators.note: varieties, plural, asks for more than one different version, so the word meat is rearranged twice

explanation.surface: A butcher's selection of meats offered to a sporting colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Varieties of' wants two different shufflings of MEAT, one after the other: TEAM and MATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A colleague on the same side in a game is a fellow player.

parts.note: reads like a gatecrasher walking into a workplace, but office means a position of power such as a throne

explanation.definitionFit: A usurper seizes a position of authority, such as a crown, without any right to it.

indicators.note: a treatment works something over, so these letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A gentle remedy given to pets at the vet.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaniels are a family of dog breeds, such as the cocker.

explanation.surface: An instruction to do something disgusting.
explanation.definitionFit: To make money is to be paid it, and to gross a sum is to receive it as income before deductions.

explanation.surface: A path to walk along rather than drive.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved opening is a passage under a bridge or gateway, and also the raised curve of the sole of the human foot.

clue.text: Tax put on new car stock

indicators.note: new implies a fresh version, so these letters are remade in another order

parts.note: VAT is value added tax, the UK sales tax

explanation.surface: Sales tax is added to new car stock in the showroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' is the anagram signal and 'put on' places the tax after it. 'stock' looks like showroom inventory but is an old-fashioned neckcloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock is a wide neckband or neckcloth, an old-fashioned form of tie.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'A portion of rhubarb jam' reads as a double definition giving STICK (a stick of rhubarb; to jam), not the printed STUCK, and no crossing grid is available to confirm which the grid holds.

clue.text: It's becoming a type of fraction

explanation.surface: Something becoming a fraction of what it was.
explanation.definitionFit: Becoming here means seemly or fitting; a fraction whose numerator is smaller than its denominator, like three-quarters, also carries this name.

definitions.note: singular where the answer is plural: walls built as defences

parts.note: a ramp is a swindle or racket
arts are skills, as in the arts of war

explanation.surface: A tennis player uses racket skills to defend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used in' links the wordplay to the definition; 'Racket' is a swindle, a RAMP, not a tennis bat.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramparts are the broad earth or stone walls built around a fort to protect it.

parts.note: US is short for United States, so American
read as Gate's head, the first letter of gate

explanation.surface: Hiring an American to work in Gateshead.
explanation.walkthrough: Gateshead is a town in north-east England, but split as 'Gate's head' it gives G.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean making use of something or someone to do a job.

clue.text: River lighter may transfer the ashes

parts.note: the Test is a river in Hampshire, famous for trout
a match is something for lighting a fire

explanation.surface: Something by the river to light a fire may move the ashes.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the cricket series between England and Australia; a win in one of its games can move the trophy. The Test is a Hampshire river.
explanation.definitionFit: A game in the England-Australia series decides which side holds the famous urn, so one can pass it over.
